summary: Santa Clara County peak with a lookout by June 1926 (Charles Scott); FFLA lists it gone, but an undated climbing guide describes a tower still standing; the guide names two landowners on the route, not the summit's owner.

facts.status_note: FFLA lists it as gone; an undated climbing guide describes an abandoned two-story wooden tower still standing at the summit

events.note: Charles Scott named as the lookout on Eylar Mountain in a 22 June 1926 Oakland Tribune report, as quoted by Forest Lookouts
Forest fire burned three days on Eylar Mountain; more than 1000 acres of brush burned near Devil Hoe canyon; reported extinguished

evidence.supports: northernmost Diablo Range peak above 4,000 feet
evidence.quote: Eylar Mountain is the most northern of the Diablo Range peaks that stand above 4,000 feet.

evidence.supports: fourth highest peak in Santa Clara County
evidence.quote: It is also the fourth highest peak in Santa Clara County

evidence.supports: Charles Scott lookout on Eylar Mountain; prairie fire put out Sunday, thought to have started the larger blaze
evidence.quote: Charles Scott , lookout on Eylar mountain, extinguished a prairie fire Sunday afternoon which now is thought to have started the larger blaze.

evidence.supports: larger fire burned three days, threatened a manganese mine, reported extinguished
evidence.quote: Brought under control by a fire squad of 12 men, the forest fire that has been burning for three days on Eylar mountain, and which today threatened to spread to a manganese mine, was reported extinguished.

evidence.supports: more than 1000 acres of brush burned near Devil Hoe canyon
evidence.quote: More than 1000 acres of brush were burned near Devil Hoe canyon

evidence.supports: fire was on the Alameda-Santa Clara county line
evidence.quote: The blaze was on the Alameda-Santa Clara county line.

evidence.supports: FFLA lists Eylar Mountain lookout as Gone
climbing guide: fire road to summit; abandoned two-story wooden tower still stands
evidence.quote: A fire road leads directly to the summit where an abandoned, two-story wooden tower still stands.

evidence.supports: cement platform or foundation north of the tower
evidence.quote: There is also a cement platform or foundation north of the tower.

evidence.supports: guide's route crawls under a fence marked with a buried electrical cable sign
evidence.quote: crawl under the fence that has a small yellow sign indicating buried electrical cable

evidence.supports: guide names two landowners at gates on the route; does not name the summit's owner
evidence.quote: The first encloses land owned by N3 Cattle Company. The second indicates land owned by Biel Property, Inc.

notes_for_editor: Unresolved conflict: FFLA lists the lookout as gone (no date); an undated SummitPost climbing guide says an abandoned tower still stands. The guide names two landowners at gates on the route (N3 Cattle Company; Biel Property, Inc.) but does not say who owns the summit. The guide's route crosses a fence, so the story gives no route directions, only a warning about the fence. Record kind 'unknown' and FFLA type 'Unknown' are both left unchanged. The 1926 fire comes from a Tribune report quoted on Forest Lookouts; the original paper was not read.
